summary: Provides a functional description of the signaling extensions needed for Generalized MPLS. GMPLS extends the MPLS control plane to time-division networks such as SONET and SDH, wavelength switching with optical lambdas, and spatial switching between ports or fibers.

plainLanguage.summary: MPLS sets up labelled paths for packets. Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) extends the same idea to equipment that forwards by time slot, by wavelength of light, or by whole fiber, none of which carry packet headers. This RFC describes what the signaling must do, in a form that any signaling protocol can implement; the concrete message formats are published separately.

questions: what is a label set in gmpls
subtitle: The protocol-independent description of how GMPLS signals paths over time slots, wavelengths and fibers.

tldr.problem: MPLS assumed every Label Switching Router could read packet or cell headers, but equipment that forwards by time slot, wavelength or physical port has no such header to read.
tldr.mechanism: Generalized MPLS defines a Generalized Label Request, a Generalized Label, label sets, suggested labels, bidirectional paths, protection and administrative status information, and interface identification, all without tying the formats to one signaling protocol.
tldr.outcome: It is the functional description of GMPLS signaling; the wire formats live in RFC 3473 for RSVP-TE and RFC 3472 for CR-LDP. It is a Proposed Standard that nine later RFCs have updated.

facts.label: Bandwidth encoding
facts.value: 32-bit IEEE floating point, bytes per second

today: RFC 3471 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the functional description of GMPLS signaling. It has been updated by RFC 4201, RFC 4328, RFC 4872, RFC 6002, RFC 6003, RFC 6205, RFC 7074, RFC 7699 and RFC 8359. The wire formats live in RFC 3473 for RSVP-TE and in RFC 3472 for CR-LDP.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needed Generalizing
sections.content:
The Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) architecture, RFC 3031, supports forwarding data based on a label. Its Label Switching Routers (LSRs) were assumed to have a forwarding plane that can recognize packet or cell boundaries and process packet or cell headers. The architecture was then extended to LSRs whose forwarding plane recognizes neither packets nor cells, because the forwarding decision is based on time slots, wavelengths or physical ports.

The RFC sorts interfaces into four classes:

  • Packet-Switch Capable (PSC): recognizes packet or cell boundaries and forwards on header content, for example routers using the MPLS shim header or ATM LSRs using the VPI/VCI.
  • Time-Division Multiplex Capable (TDM): forwards by the data's time slot in a repeating cycle, for example a SONET/SDH cross-connect.
  • Lambda Switch Capable (LSC): forwards by the wavelength on which data arrives, for example an optical cross-connect at the level of an individual wavelength.
  • Fiber-Switch Capable (FSC): forwards by position in physical space, for example an optical cross-connect at the level of a single or multiple fibers.

Nested LSPs let the system scale: FSC at the top, then LSC, TDM and PSC, so a packet LSP can ride inside a TDM LSP, which rides inside a wavelength LSP, which rides inside a fiber LSP. The document is only a functional description. Protocol-specific formats are in RFC 3473 (RSVP-TE) and RFC 3472 (CR-LDP), and technology-specific details are left to other documents. Generalized MPLS differs from traditional MPLS in more than the switching types: an LSP must start and end on a similar type of LSR, the payload of an LSP can itself be something like SONET/SDH or 1 or 10Gb Ethernet, and bandwidth on non-packet links can be allocated only in discrete units, with far fewer labels available than on packet links.
sections.plainLanguage: Some machines cannot read labels on packages; they only know which time slot, color of light or fiber the data arrives on. GMPLS teaches label-style signaling to work for them too, and this RFC lists what the signaling must be able to say.

sections.title: Label Formats for Every Switching Type
sections.content:
To widen MPLS into the optical and time domain, several new forms of label are required. They are collectively called a generalized label: a value with enough information for the receiving node to program its cross-connect, whatever the type, so the ingress segments of the path are properly joined. Since both ends know what kind of link they are using, the generalized label has no type field; the type is implicit in the link.

The Generalized Label Request carries three fields. The 8-bit LSP Encoding Type says how the data on the path is encoded (Packet is 1, Ethernet 2, ANSI/ETSI PDH 3, SDH or SONET 5, Digital Wrapper 7, Lambda 8, Fiber 9, FiberChannel 11); it represents the nature of the path, not of the links it crosses. The 8-bit Switching Type says what switching is requested on a link, needed when a link advertises more than one capability (PSC-1 to PSC-4 are values 1 to 4, L2SC is 51, TDM is 100, LSC is 150 and FSC is 200). The 16-bit G-PID identifies the payload, that is the client layer of the path, used by the endpoints and sometimes the penultimate hop; standard Ethertype values are used for packet and Ethernet paths. Bandwidth encodings ride in a 32-bit number in IEEE floating point format, in bytes per second, with guideline values from DS0 up to OC-768/STM-256.

The Generalized Label has a variable-length label field whose interpretation depends on the link. It may represent a single fiber in a bundle, a waveband, a wavelength, a set of time slots, or a generic MPLS, Frame Relay or ATM label. It carries a single level of label; layered paths are established as separate LSPs. For fiber and lambda switching a port or wavelength label is 32 bits, meaningful only between two neighbors, so a receiver may convert it to a locally significant value. A Waveband Label adds a 32-bit Waveband Id chosen by the sender, plus a Start Label and End Label for the lowest and highest wavelengths in the band; a waveband can later be subdivided into wavelengths, so it acts as one more level of label.

A Suggested Label gives a downstream node the upstream node's label preference, so the upstream node can start configuring hardware early. This is only an optimization: the downstream node keeps control of the label, and an ingress node should not transmit data on a suggested label until the downstream node passes a label upstream. A Label Set limits the downstream node's choices. Its 8-bit Action field selects an inclusive list (0), exclusive list (1), inclusive range (2) or exclusive range (3), where a range bound of zero means no bound; a 14-bit Label Type names the label format; the subchannels use the generalized label format. Without a Label Set, all labels in the valid range may be used.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask for a path you say how the data is encoded, what kind of switching you want, and what payload rides inside. The answer is a label that can name a packet tag, a time slot, a wavelength or a whole fiber, and a label set is the list of labels the far side may pick from.

sections.title: Bidirectional Label Switched Paths
sections.content:
Traditional MPLS traffic engineering, and even LDP, is unidirectional. Generalized MPLS supports bidirectional LSPs, which have the same traffic engineering requirements in each direction, including fate sharing, protection and restoration, the same routers, and the same resource requirements such as latency and jitter. The node that starts establishment is the initiator; the target is the terminator.

Building a two-way path as two separate one-way setups has real costs. Setup latency equals a full round trip plus signaling transit time, and the worst-case delay for discovering a failed setup doubles. Control overhead is twice that of a one-way path, because separate messages are generated for each segment. Resources are established in separate segments, which complicates route selection and adds races when resources are assigned, lowering the chance of success. It is also harder to give SONET/SDH equipment, which may rely on bidirectional hop-by-hop paths for protection switching, a clean interface, and many optical service providers consider bidirectional lightpaths a requirement. With bidirectional LSPs, both directions are established with a single set of signaling messages, so setup latency is essentially one round trip plus processing, and the message count matches a one-way path. Two labels are allocated; setup is indicated by an Upstream Label object or TLV with the same format as the generalized label.

Two setups travelling in opposite directions can contend for the same labels. If labels are unrestricted and alternates exist, each node passes a different label upstream and the contention resolves itself. When resources are restricted, the node with the higher node ID wins the contention, and the other node MUST issue a PathErr or NOTIFICATION with a "Routing problem/Label allocation failure" indication and SHOULD retry with a different upstream label. Policies can reduce the chance of collisions: the lower-numbered node never suggests a downstream label and always accepts a suggested label from a higher-numbered node, and the two ends allocate from opposite ends of the label range. One RSVP special case matters: the neighbor's node ID might not be known when the first Path message is sent, so a node should suggest a label chosen at random from the available label space.
sections.plainLanguage: Two one-way paths do not make a good two-way circuit: they are slower to set up, use twice the messages, and can collide. GMPLS sets both directions up in one exchange, with rules that decide who keeps a contested label.

sections.title: Label Errors and Explicit Label Control
sections.content:
Errors carrying an "Unacceptable label value" indication occur in both traditional MPLS and GMPLS. When they do, the node generating the error can say which labels it would have accepted, using an Acceptable Label Set. Its format is identical to a Label Set, and the protocol-specific documents say which error messages carry it.

Explicit label control covers the case where the existing explicit route semantics are not precise enough. A traditional Explicit Route Object can include a particular node or interface and terminate a path on a particular outgoing interface, but it cannot name the label to use on a link. That matters when the initiator of a path wants to select the label on a specific link, for example when two paths are spliced together, with the tail of the first joined to the head of the second, a case more likely on non-packet links. The Label ERO subobject and the matching ER Hop are introduced for this. The L bit must be set to 0. The U bit gives the direction of the label: 0 for the downstream label, and 1 for the upstream label, used only on bidirectional paths. The Label field has the same format as the label field in the Generalized Label. How these subobjects are placed and ordered in a message is specific to each signaling protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: When a label is rejected, the receiver can answer with a shortlist of labels it would accept. And when a planner wants to choose the exact label on one link, perhaps to join two paths end to end, a new subobject carries that choice inside the explicit route.

sections.title: Protection and Administrative Status
sections.content:
Protection Information is carried in a new object or TLV, and its use is optional. It indicates the link protection attributes requested for a path, currently the desired link protection type. If a particular protection type, such as 1+1 or 1:N, is requested, the connection request is processed only if that type can be honored. Protection capabilities of a link may be advertised in routing, and path computation algorithms may take them into account. The Secondary (S) bit marks a secondary path: a backup to a primary, whose resources are not used until the primary fails. Until then, other paths MAY use the resources of the secondary; at failover, any path using them MUST be preempted.

The 6-bit Link Flags field names the acceptable protection types. A value of zero means any, including no, link protection; more than one bit may be set when several types are acceptable, and the final choice is a local policy decision. The defined flags are 0x20 Enhanced (a scheme more reliable than Dedicated 1+1, for example 4 fiber BLSR/MS-SPRING), 0x10 Dedicated 1+1, 0x08 Dedicated 1:1, 0x04 Shared (such as 1:N), 0x02 Unprotected, and 0x01 Extra Traffic, which lets a path use links that protect other traffic, accepting that it may be preempted when the protected traffic's links fail.

Administrative Status Information, also in a new object or TLV and also optional, is used in two ways. First, it reports the administrative state of a path: up or down, in a testing mode, and whether deletion is in progress. What a node does with the state is a local decision, for example inhibiting alarm reporting while a path is down or in testing, or reporting alarms at a priority of at most Non service affecting. Second, it carries a request to set a path's administrative state; such a request is always relayed to the ingress node, which acts on it. The object holds a Reflect (R) bit, which asks the edge node to reflect the object back, a Testing (T) bit, an Administratively down (A) bit, and a Deletion in progress (D) bit.
sections.plainLanguage: Two status fields ride with the signaling. One says what kind of backup the link should provide, and whether the path is itself a backup. The other says whether the path is up, in testing, down on purpose or being deleted, and can ask the sender to change that state.

sections.title: Control Channels Separate from Data
sections.content:
The idea of a control channel different from the data channel entered MPLS with link bundling. In GMPLS the separation may have many causes, including data channels that cannot carry in-band control information. Two issues follow: how signaling identifies the data channel being controlled, and how control channel failures that do not touch the data channels are handled.

In traditional MPLS the association of control channel to data channel is implicitly one-to-one, so no extra information is needed. When that association is absent, GMPLS carries interface identification information. Identification schemes include IPv4 or IPv6 addresses, interface indexes, and component interfaces established by configuration or by a protocol such as LMP; in all cases the upstream node names the data interface using addresses and identifiers that it uses itself. The information is a list of TLVs. Each TLV's Length counts the whole TLV in octets, and a value field that is not a multiple of four is zero-padded for four-octet alignment. The Type field names the interface kind: 1 is IPv4, 2 is IPv6, 3 is an interface index, 4 is a downstream component interface and 5 is an upstream component interface. For types 3, 4 and 5 the value holds a 32-bit IP Address and a 32-bit Interface ID; the special value 0xFFFFFFFF means the same label is valid across all component links.

Two faults must be handled once control is independent of data. In the first, a failure limits neighboring nodes' ability to pass control messages for a period; after communication is restored, the signaling protocol must show that both nodes kept their state, and must synchronize any state changes made during the failure. In the second, a node's control plane fails and restarts having lost most of its state; then both neighbors must resynchronize with it, and the restarting node must have preserved some information, such as its mapping of incoming to outgoing labels. Each signaling protocol handles these cases in its own way, in RFC 3473 and RFC 3472. The cases apply only when data channel failures can be detected independently of control channel failures.
sections.plainLanguage: When the signaling wires run on their own, the message must name the data wire it controls, using the sender's own addresses. And when the signaling fails but the data keeps flowing, the protocol must let neighbors keep their state and re-synchronize afterwards.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document introduces no new security considerations to either RFC 3212 (Constraint-Based LSP Setup using LDP) or RFC 3209 (RSVP-TE). The security considerations mentioned in those two documents apply to the respective protocol-specific forms of GMPLS, which are RFC 3473 for RSVP-TE and RFC 3472 for CR-LDP.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC adds no new security rules of its own. The security rules of the two signaling protocols it builds on carry over to their GMPLS versions.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content: The RFC creates five number spaces, administered by IANA, with future assignments allocated through IETF Consensus action or documented in a Specification. The LSP Encoding Type is 8 bits with a valid range of 1 to 255, of which this document defines values 1 to 11. The Switching Type is 8 bits with a valid range of 1 to 255, of which this document defines values 1 to 4, 100, 150 and 200. The Generalized PID (G-PID) is 16 bits with a valid range of 0 to 1500, of which this document defines values 0 to 46. The Action field of the Label Set is 8 bits with a valid range of 0 to 255, of which this document defines values 0 to 3. The Interface_ID Type is 16 bits with a valid range of 1 to 65535, of which this document defines values 1 to 5.
sections.plainLanguage: Every number field this RFC defines gets an official registry, with a stated range and the values this document fills in. IANA keeps those registries so that all implementations use the same numbers.

fields.name: LSP Encoding Type
fields.desc: How the path's data is encoded: Packet is 1, Ethernet 2, SDH or SONET 5, Lambda 8, Fiber 9.

fields.name: Switching Type
fields.desc: The switching wanted on a link, such as TDM 100, LSC 150 or FSC 200.

fields.name: G-PID
fields.desc: Identifier of the payload, the client layer of the path.

items.title: Setup latency
items.text: One round trip instead of two separate one-way setups.

items.title: Control overhead
items.text: The same number of messages as a single one-way path.

items.title: Route selection
items.text: No races between two segments established independently.

items.title: Protection switching
items.text: A clean interface for SONET/SDH equipment that uses bidirectional hop-by-hop paths.

items.title: Optical services
items.text: Many optical providers require bidirectional lightpaths.

items.label: Enhanced
items.desc: More reliable than Dedicated 1+1, for example 4 fiber BLSR/MS-SPRING.

items.label: Dedicated 1+1
items.desc: A dedicated 1+1 link layer protection scheme.

items.label: Dedicated 1:1
items.desc: A dedicated 1:1 link layer protection scheme.

items.label: Shared
items.desc: A shared scheme such as 1:N protection.

items.label: Extra Traffic
items.desc: Uses links that protect other traffic; may be preempted at failover.
